opus-5.5.text:
Well, the short answer is that smell was the one major sense that machine learning just hadn't touched. If you look at vision, we've had decades of work, from color science all the way to modern computer vision. We understand how wavelengths of light map to perceived color, and that relationship is captured in things like the RGB color space. For hearing, we understand that pitch relates to frequency. But for smell, there was no equivalent. If I hand you a molecule's structure, nobody could reliably tell you what it would smell like. That's been an open problem in chemistry and neuroscience for something like seventy or a hundred years.

So the motivation was really: can we build the equivalent of a color map, but for odor? A space where molecules that smell similar sit close together, and where you can go from a chemical structure to a prediction of how it smells. If you can do that, you've digitized a sense that's never been digitized before.

The other part was that the timing was right. Graph neural networks had matured to the point where you could naturally represent molecules as graphs, atoms as nodes and bonds as edges, and learn directly from that structure instead of hand-engineering features. And there were datasets, from the flavor and fragrance industry, where expert perfumers had labeled thousands of molecules with descriptors like "fruity," "woody," "garlicky." Put those together and you can actually train a model.

When we did, the embedding space that came out had this really beautiful structure. Related odors clustered together, and it generalized to molecules the model had never seen. Later we showed in a head-to-head that the model's predictions could be as good as, or better than, an individual trained human panelist at describing a new molecule. That told us this wasn't just a curiosity. There's a learnable, structured relationship between chemistry and perception, and mapping it opens the door to things like discovering new scent molecules, better insect repellents, and eventually maybe giving computers a sense of smell.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the honest answer is that it started as a personal obsession long before it was a research agenda. I've been fascinated by smell since I was a kid, and when I got into neuroscience, what struck me was how lopsided our understanding of the senses is. We have incredibly mature theories of vision and hearing. We know that color lives on a wavelength axis, we know that pitch is frequency. You can draw a map. For smell, we had nothing like that. We had no idea what the axes even were.

And that's actually a really strange situation when you think about it. Olfaction is arguably the oldest sense. Bacteria sense chemicals. Every organism on the planet has some way of detecting molecules in its environment. And yet if you asked a chemist to look at a molecule and tell you what it smells like, they mostly couldn't, except through experience and intuition. There's no first-principles theory. Two molecules can look nearly identical structurally and smell completely different, and two that look totally unrelated can smell almost the same. So the structure-to-percept problem was just wide open.

What made Google Brain the right place to attack it was that this is fundamentally a machine learning problem dressed up as a chemistry problem. A molecule is a graph. Atoms are nodes, bonds are edges. And right around that time, graph neural networks were getting good enough that you could learn representations directly from molecular structure instead of hand-engineering features. So the question became: if you train a model to predict odor descriptors from structure, does the thing it learns internally look like a sensory map? Does it have the kind of organization we see in color space or in tonotopic maps in the auditory system?

And the exciting part was that the embedding the model learned turned out to be meaningful. Molecules that smell similar cluster together, even when their chemistry diverges, and the map generalizes to molecules it's never seen. That was the moment where it felt less like a curiosity and more like we'd found a real coordinate system for a sense that never had one. The longer-term vision is that if you can digitize smell, you unlock a whole category of applications, from diagnosing disease on the breath to designing safer, more sustainable fragrance molecules. But the starting point was really just a very old scientific question that finally had the right tools available to make progress on it.

astra-6.text:
I was fascinated by this gap in our understanding of the senses. For vision, we have ways to organize light by wavelength, and for hearing, we can organize sound by frequency. With smell, we don’t have an equivalent map that tells us how two molecules relate to each other perceptually—whether they’ll smell similar or completely different.

That makes it a really interesting machine learning problem. You have the structure of a molecule on one side and someone’s experience of its smell on the other. Could we learn the relationship between those two things, and build a representation where distance actually means something about how things smell?

The reason to focus on a map was that it could be foundational. Rather than solve one narrow prediction problem, we wanted a way to organize the space that could help us ask—and eventually answer—lots of different questions about olfaction.

sol-6.1.text:
What fascinated me was that smell is this incredibly rich sense, but we don’t have a good map of it. With vision, we can organize colors by wavelength. With sound, we have frequency. But if I show you two molecules, it’s very hard to predict whether they’ll smell similar—or even whether they’ll have a smell at all.

So the question was: could we use machine learning to connect molecular structure to what people actually perceive? Could we build a space where things that smell alike are close together, even if their chemical structures look quite different?

Google Brain was a great place to explore that because learning useful representations was such a central part of the work. And a map felt foundational. If we could organize smell in a meaningful way, we’d have a starting point for predicting it, measuring it, and eventually doing more useful things with it.
